chunks: "I group the sources into three buckets. The first is resistive: any DC or low-frequency current through ground copper makes an IR drop.
5 amps across three squares of one-ounce copper, which is about half a milliohm per square, gives about 7 millivolts, and neck-downs, thin traces, vias and connector pins make it much worse.
The second is inductive, which is usually the bigger one on fast boards. Every time current changes quickly through any ground path, you get L di/dt.
That happens when many outputs switch at once, called ground bounce or SSN, with switching regulators and their hot loops, through package ground pins and through connectors and cables.
A nanohenry with a 1 amp per nanosecond edge is a volt.

The third is everything that changes the path or injects voltage: slots, splits and via fields that force return currents to detour, shared return paths between noisy and quiet circuits, magnetic pickup in ground loops, capacitive coupling from nearby noisy nodes, and resonances of the power-ground plane pair.
Even external things like ESD events or a cable connected to a different ground can inject voltage.
Once I know which bucket it is, the cure is different: more copper, smaller loops and better decoupling, or breaking the loop."
